analysis.one_liner: Lets people take race discrimination claims to court instead of forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee from May 2, 2023 until the Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with 49 House Democrats and no Republicans backing it.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies often require workers, tenants, and customers to sign agreements giving up their right to sue in court and instead take disputes to a private arbitrator chosen under the company's process. This bill would let anyone alleging race, color, or national origin discrimination or harassment choose to bypass that agreement and bring the case in court, including as a class or collective action. A judge, not an arbitrator, would decide whether the law applies.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, tenants, and customers who signed mandatory arbitration clauses and later faced race discrimination, harassment, or retaliation, plus coworkers who could join class actions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People facing race discrimination with arbitration clauses

how_it_helps.text: A person alleging race discrimination, including harassment or retaliation, on the basis of race, color, or national origin could elect to have a predispute arbitration agreement or class-action waiver declared invalid in that case [S2][S3].
The claim could be filed in court under federal, tribal, state, or local law, and could proceed as a class or collective action, since joint-action waivers are also invalidated [S3].
A court, not an arbitrator, would decide whether the law applies and whether the arbitration agreement is enforceable, even if the contract tried to delegate that question to an arbitrator [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers and other companies that rely on mandatory arbitration clauses would face jury trials and class actions in race discrimination cases, and the private arbitration industry would lose that business.

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only race, color, and national origin discrimination, leaving arbitration clauses fully enforceable for other civil rights claims such as disability, religion, sex (before the 2022 law), age, or pay [S3].

By design it pushes these cases into court, so employers would lose the generally faster, private, lower-cost arbitration track, and workers would take on litigation costs that arbitration sometimes avoids; supporters judge that a fair trade for jury access and class actions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people facing race discrimination, the benefit is real: a day in court before a judge and jury, and the ability to join with coworkers. The costs fall mainly on companies, though some claimants who prefer a quick, cheap arbitration would instead face slower court litigation. The bill's narrow scope limits both its help and its disruption.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Colin Allred, joined by Rep. Hank Johnson of Georgia, introduced the bill on May 2, 2023 [S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and no further action was ever taken [S5].
It drew 49 cosponsors, all House Democrats [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with mandatory arbitration clauses keep routing race discrimination claims into private arbitration, and the arbitration industry keeps the business.

for.name: Rep. Colin Z. Allred
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee on May 2, 2023

for.name: Rep. Hank Johnson
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction of the bill

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican in this Congress
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing, markup, or vote for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: All 49 cosponsors were House Democrats and none of the House's 224 Republicans signed on; after referral to the committee on May 2, 2023, no further action was taken [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would let their workers, tenants, and customers take race discrimination claims to court instead of private arbitration, exposing them to jury trials and class actions. Their interest in keeping disputes private and low-cost runs against claimants' access to court.
Race discrimination cases could no longer be forced into their fee-based process at the claimant's election, removing a category of business. The public's alternative is a public courtroom.
